Leaders | Pick your phantom

Either AI or public debt could crash markets. Butprobably not both

If AI stocks collapse, bond yields will fall

Oct 22nd 2026

Two SPECTRES stalk financial markets. One is the fear that surging bondyields will make the rich world’s shaky public finances unsustainable,triggering a nasty fiscal crisis. The other is the worry that the revenues fromartificial intelligence needed to keep the data-centre boom going will fail toarrive. As we report, that would devastate credit markets and cause a big fallin stocks, too.

The good news is that only an Ichabod Crane would think that both thesescenarios could strike at once. Instead, investors must decide which story isscarier. For now, The Economist is more worried about sovereign debt.

For most of the year, concerns about governments have dominated. Betweenthe end of February and the start of October, the yield on 30-year USTreasuries rose by a full percentage point. The Iran war has sent inflation upand forced central banks to raise interest rates. Strong economic growth andthe rush to build data centres have caused a scramble for capital in whichgovernments have had to compete with the private sector. In Japan, Britainand especially France, investors have fretted about the ability ofgovernments to service their debts.

In recent weeks, though, the prospect of an end to the AI boom has scaredthe markets more. The five-year bonds of CoreWeave, a “neocloud” thatrents out data centres, trade at a 15% yield, up from 10% in July. Thecompany’s share price has fallen by about a third in the past month. Theslowing revenue growth of Anthropic, an AI-model provider, has investorsworried that the cash CoreWeave and its peers need may not arrive, or atleast not quickly enough to pay their creditors. Interlinked financing meansthat pain could spread quickly, through both the ai supply chain and theprivate-credit and insurance firms that hold a lot of data-centre debt.

As a result, many sovereign bonds have rallied. There has been little relieffor France, where riots are worsening a political crisis, or Britain, where anupcoming budget makes investors nervous. But yields on ten-year Treasuries

are down by a fifth of a point. Investors usually flee to the safety ofAmerican bonds in a downturn. Everywhere else, as data-centre investmentslowed, an AI crash would ease the scramble for capital. And it would leadcentral banks to lower interest rates to support growth, thereby making debtseasier to service.

Only in a big crash akin to the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2007-09would the two risks collide. Governments are already sufficiently in the redthat a deep recession would, by collapsing tax revenues and increasingwelfare spending, make budget deficits look truly terrifying. Long-termbond yields might rise even as short-term interest rates fell—a nastysymptom of fiscal malaise that sometimes strikes emerging markets. It didnot happen during the GFC, but the starting-point for debt and deficits todayis higher.

Thankfully, there is no reason to expect such a deep crash. True, the historyof finance shows that useful new technologies often bring about a boom andbust, and the web of financing behind AI has become complex. But theindustry’s interlinkages are better understood than the alphabet-soup ofhousing-market securities was in 2007. Banks are safer, too. Though theyare exposed to ai via their lending to private-credit firms, their balancesheets are less fragile and better monitored. And backstopping much of theindustry is the chipmaker Nvidia, which has an enormous cash pile. Mostimportant, AI assets, though a big slice of many stock indices, are a smallerchunk of household wealth than housing.

So the best comparison for today’s AI vulnerabilities remains the dotcombubble of the late 1990s. When it burst in 2000, cratering stocks caused onlya mild recession. Bond yields came down, too, and underlying productivitygrowth held up. Such a scenario would hardly solve governments’ long-termbudget problems, but it might forestall them. Many economies outsideAmerica are less exposed to the AI boom than they are to bond yields;growth falling by less than interest rates would make legacy debts a lighterburden. America’s deficit would grow in a recession, but so would theworld’s appetite for Treasuries, because the dollar is the world’s reservecurrency.

By contrast, if high interest rates triggered a sovereign-debt blow-up theconsequences would be truly grave. If investors lost confidence inTreasuries, it would threaten the dollar’s valuable status as a haven. AsFrance is discovering, trying to close big deficits under duress can lead topolitical instability. Governments may prefer to inflate away debt than to payit down. That could imperil the stability on which all investment depends. Arun on sovereign debt in a big advanced economy could well leave investorswishing that a dotcom-style ai bust was all they had to worry about. ■
